title: Nonsurgical Therapy for Hydrocephalus: A Comprehensive and Critical Review

subsections.section_title: Pathophysiological Foundations and Therapeutic Targets in Hydrocephalus
subsections.subsection_title: Pathophysiological Foundations and Therapeutic Targets in Hydrocephalus - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Hydrocephalus is best framed as a disorder of the integrated cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) system rather than a simple imbalance between choroid plexus secretion and arachnoid villus absorption. Contemporary descriptions of CSF dynamics emphasize distributed production, complex intracranial and spinal circulation, pressure-dependent compliance, and multiple egress pathways, challenging the classical “bulk flow” model as a complete explanation for ventricular enlargement ref [10], ref [22], ref [39]. This broader view is essential for nonsurgical therapy because it expands therapeutic targets beyond CSF formation alone.

A central pathophysiological feature is the coupling of CSF motion to cerebral blood volume changes and tissue biomechanics. Cardiac-driven pulsatility propagates through the ventricular and subarachnoid spaces, and abnormal transmission of these pulsations can contribute to ventricular distension, altered periventricular stress, and impaired intracranial compliance ref [19], ref [30]. Mathematical and physiological models therefore support hydrocephalus as a disorder of the blood-CSF-brain unit, in which pressure waves, venous outflow, and viscoelastic properties of brain tissue shape disease expression as much as static resistance to flow ref [10], ref [30].

Equally important, CSF clearance occurs through anatomically diverse outflow routes, including arachnoid pathways, cranial and spinal nerve-associated routes, and lymphatic drainage systems ref [4], ref [57]. Water transport proteins such as aquaporins further modulate fluid exchange across ependymal and glial interfaces, linking barrier physiology to edema, ventricular expansion, and potentially pharmacologic intervention ref [58]. Taken together, these mechanisms identify several nonsurgical targets: reduction of CSF secretion, modulation of pulsatility and compliance, enhancement of lymphatic or alternative outflow, and regulation of transcellular water transport ref [4], ref [57], ref [58].

subsections.section_title: Pathophysiological Foundations and Therapeutic Targets in Hydrocephalus
subsections.subsection_title: Pathophysiological Foundations and Therapeutic Targets in Hydrocephalus - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A central pathophysiological theme in hydrocephalus is that ventricular enlargement cannot be explained solely by bulk overproduction or a simple fixed obstruction model; rather, it emerges from disturbed coupling among CSF pulsatility, compliance, tissue mechanics, and reabsorption pathways. Historical reappraisals of CSF physiology have challenged the classical circulation doctrine and emphasized distributed fluid exchange and pressure-wave transmission across the craniospinal system, reframing hydrocephalus as a disorder of hydrodynamic imbalance and altered brain-fluid interaction rather than only failed drainage ref [15], ref [54], ref [55].

Experimental and imaging studies support this broader biomechanical view. Reduced CSF reabsorption has been linked to progressive ventricular dilation through altered intracranial pressure-volume relationships and impaired damping of pulsatile forces ref [14]. Ventricle wall motion appears to participate actively in abnormal intraventricular flow patterns, indicating that the ependymal boundary is mechanically responsive and may contribute to tissue strain and periventricular injury ref [14]. In communicating hydrocephalus, ventricular morphology also correlates with aqueductal flow metrics, suggesting that geometry, pulsatile flow, and compliance reciprocally shape disease evolution rather than acting as independent variables ref [49].

These concepts are reinforced by computational and animal models. Coupled poroelastic-CFD frameworks show that ventricular distension depends on both fluid movement and parenchymal material properties, providing a mechanistic basis for therapies aimed at compliance, edema, or interstitial fluid transport ref [34]. Likewise, chronic TGF-β1 mouse models demonstrate measurable CSF flow abnormalities in fibrosis-associated hydrocephalus, linking inflammatory extracellular matrix remodeling to disturbed hydrodynamics ref [52]. Collectively, these studies identify therapeutic targets beyond shunting, including enhancement of reabsorption, modulation of pulsatility transmission, reduction of fibrotic remodeling, and protection of the mechanically stressed ventricular wall ref [14], ref [52], ref [54].

subsections.section_title: Pathophysiological Foundations and Therapeutic Targets in Hydrocephalus
subsections.subsection_title: Pathophysiological Foundations and Therapeutic Targets in Hydrocephalus - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A central therapeutic question in hydrocephalus is whether ventricular enlargement is driven predominantly by impaired cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) absorption, altered pressure-volume compensation, or disturbed vascular-CSF coupling. Infusion-based studies have therefore focused on resistance or conductance to CSF outflow as measurable surrogates of absorptive reserve. Constant-pressure infusion methods were developed to estimate CSF outflow conductance with real-time assessment of measurement reliability, strengthening the physiological interpretation of these tests in individual patients ref [16]. In chronic hydrocephalus, impaired absorption at the vertex has been attributed either to dysfunction at arachnoid granulations or to an adverse venous pressure gradient, emphasizing that the absorptive defect may be distal to CSF formation and tightly linked to venous hemodynamics ref [25].

This framework is especially relevant in normal-pressure hydrocephalus (NPH), where elevated outflow resistance has been associated with characteristic CSF dynamic abnormalities and with subsequent shunt responsiveness in some patient series ref [28]. However, the relationship between intracranial pressure (ICP) and outflow resistance remains controversial. Some analyses suggest that measured outflow resistance depends on the prevailing ICP during testing ref [44], whereas others found no consistent relationship in NPH ref [46]. These discrepancies imply that absorptive failure is not a single static lesion but may vary with compliance, venous pressure, and the testing paradigm itself ref [16], ref [28], ref [44], ref [46].

Beyond mean pressure, pulsatile and osmotic factors may also define actionable pathophysiology. CSF pulse pressure methods were proposed as a proxy for vasogenic B-wave activity ref [22], and vasogenic ICP waves have been linked to increased CSF outflow resistance in NPH, supporting the concept that abnormal vascular pulsatility can worsen CSF egress ref [26]. In parallel, the hypothesis of compensated CSF hyperosmolarity suggests that osmotic disequilibrium may promote ventricular enlargement even without marked sustained pressure elevation ref [19]. Together, these studies identify several nonsurgical targets—improving absorptive conductance, reducing venous outflow limitation, modulating vascular pulsatility, and correcting osmotic imbalance—that may complement or, in selected settings, reduce dependence on diversion procedures ref [19], ref [22], ref [25], ref [26].

subsections.section_title: Pathophysiological Foundations and Therapeutic Targets in Hydrocephalus
subsections.subsection_title: Pathophysiological Foundations and Therapeutic Targets in Hydrocephalus - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A complementary view of hydrocephalus emphasizes impaired cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) egress, venous coupling, and disturbed pulsatile buffering rather than a simple excess-production model. Ex vivo work on human arachnoid granulations supports their role as pressure-dependent outflow structures, while neonatal hydrocephalus data indicate that obstruction and malabsorption often coexist early in disease, reinforcing the concept of distributed resistance across the CSF outflow pathway rather than a single anatomical block alone ref [27], ref [57].

These outflow abnormalities are tightly linked to intracranial hemodynamics. Studies of cerebral venous outflow show that venous pressure and compliance can materially influence CSF motion and pressure transmission, and modeling of pulsatile CSF hydrodynamics further indicates that abnormal compliance redistributes systolic and diastolic pressure waves in ways that promote ventricular enlargement and impaired compensation ref [51], ref [52]. Related analyses also suggest a mechanistic connection between cerebrovascular activity and CSF pressure-volume compensation, implying that therapeutic benefit may arise not only from lowering CSF volume but also from improving vascular-compliance coupling ref [17].

Brain-fluid exchange adds another therapeutic dimension. MRI-based measurements of CSF and interstitial fluid volumes in the human brain, together with tracer studies in immature hydrocephalic rats, indicate that hydrocephalus perturbs extracellular and interstitial transport, not merely bulk ventricular size ref [45], ref [29]. This supports nonsurgical strategies aimed at enhancing absorption, normalizing venous drainage, or modifying pulsatility and parenchymal fluid exchange, particularly in forms of communicating or developmental hydrocephalus where diffuse transport failure may be as important as focal obstruction ref [27], ref [51], ref [57].

subsections.section_title: Pathophysiological Foundations and Therapeutic Targets in Hydrocephalus
subsections.subsection_title: Pathophysiological Foundations and Therapeutic Targets in Hydrocephalus - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A therapeutically important theme in hydrocephalus is that impaired clearance may arise from distributed defects in absorption and drainage rather than from a single point of obstruction. Classical accounts of cerebrospinal fluid physiology emphasize that production, pulsatile movement, and resorption are coupled to venous and extracranial pathways, so disturbance at any node can elevate effective outflow resistance and promote ventricular enlargement ref [16], ref [34], ref [11]. Theoretical analyses likewise argue that hydrocephalus should be interpreted as a systems-level disorder in which compliance, pressure gradients, and drainage conductance interact dynamically rather than as a purely bulk-flow failure ref [39].

Evidence from experimental and clinical studies supports this broader view of distal clearance failure. In chronic hydrocephalus, impaired absorption at the cranial vertex may reflect not only dysfunction of arachnoid granulations but also elevated venous pressure, underscoring the importance of the venous side of the absorptive circuit ref [10]. Complementing this, a canine model demonstrated disordered arachnoid villus absorption during hydrocephalus ref [21], whereas tracer MRI in guinea pigs showed altered drainage pathways in hydrocephalic brains compared with normal controls ref [22]. Together, these observations identify venous pressure modulation, enhancement of alternative CSF egress routes, and restoration of absorptive interfaces as plausible nonsurgical targets ref [10], ref [21], ref [22].

A further mechanistic layer is developmental and secretory signaling. The subcommissural organ and related neuropeptide pathways influence CSF composition and flow-regulating biology, suggesting that some forms of hydrocephalus may involve disrupted ependymal-secretory signaling rather than only mechanical blockage ref [20]. For nonsurgical therapy, this widens the target space from pressure reduction alone to biologic interventions aimed at drainage pathway function, venous-lymphatic coupling, and neuroepithelial signaling networks that shape CSF homeostasis ref [20], ref [11], ref [39].

subsections.section_title: Pharmacological and Molecular Strategies for Nonsurgical Intervention
subsections.subsection_title: Pharmacological and Molecular Strategies for Nonsurgical Intervention - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A first class of nonsurgical strategies has aimed to pharmacologically reduce cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) formation or to alter water transport across brain barriers. However, the rationale is less straightforward than older bulk-flow models implied. Critical reassessments of hydrocephalus pathophysiology argue that ventricular enlargement cannot be understood solely as overproduction versus impaired absorption, which helps explain why simple secretion-suppressing therapies have generally underperformed clinically ref [22]. In chronic hydrocephalus, CSF production may already be downregulated, further limiting the theoretical benefit of drugs intended to suppress choroid plexus output ref [52].

This limitation is illustrated by acetazolamide, historically used to decrease CSF production. Although case-based use suggests that it can transiently reduce CSF burden in selected shunt-related settings, the evidence supports at most a niche, temporizing role rather than durable disease modification ref [55]. Interest has therefore shifted toward molecular regulators of water movement, especially aquaporins. Reviews of aquaporin biology identify AQP1 and AQP4 as plausible therapeutic targets, but also emphasize the difficulty of selectively modulating these channels without disrupting broader fluid and ion homeostasis ref [58]. In experimental hydrocephalus, AQP4 expression correlates with diffusion abnormalities and disease severity, supporting its relevance while also underscoring that it may be more a marker and mediator of parenchymal stress than an easily actionable single target ref [42].

A complementary pharmacological logic targets secondary injury rather than CSF formation itself. After neonatal intraventricular hemorrhage, hemoglobin and iron contribute to inflammatory and toxic cascades linked to posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus, suggesting opportunities for iron-handling or blood-product-directed interventions ref [51]. Similarly, persistent astrogliosis and microgliosis in hydrocephalus indicate that neuroinflammation is therapeutically relevant, although shunting data imply that some of this response is secondary to mechanical distortion and may not be fully reversible by drugs alone ref [44]. Cell-based molecular therapy has shown more encouraging preclinical signals: mesenchymal stem cells reduced the development of hydrocephalus after severe intraventricular hemorrhage, likely through anti-inflammatory and trophic effects rather than restoration of normal CSF hydrodynamics ref [21]. Overall, these studies support a shift from simplistic anti-secretory therapy toward multimodal approaches that address barrier water transport, hemorrhage-induced toxicity, and inflammatory injury, while highlighting substantial translational barriers ref [21], ref [42], ref [51], ref [58].

subsections.section_title: Pharmacological and Molecular Strategies for Nonsurgical Intervention
subsections.subsection_title: Pharmacological and Molecular Strategies for Nonsurgical Intervention - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A major molecular strategy has been to target inflammatory and profibrotic cascades that may convert hemorrhagic or age-related CSF disturbances into persistent hydrocephalus. Conceptually, this approach is supported by revised models of CSF physiology and hydrocephalus pathogenesis, which emphasize disturbed fluid exchange, extracellular matrix remodeling, and impaired clearance pathways rather than simple overproduction–obstruction dichotomies ref [54], ref [55]. Within this framework, transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) has attracted particular interest because elevated CSF levels have been documented after subarachnoid hemorrhage, in posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus of prematurity, and in idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus, suggesting a convergent profibrotic signal across etiologies ref [9], ref [12], ref [41].

Mechanistically, TGF-β1 is attractive because it links blood breakdown products and inflammatory activation to downstream matrix deposition and altered CSF hydrodynamics. Experimental work in TGF-β1-induced chronic hydrocephalic mice showed measurable abnormalities of CSF flow dynamics, providing preclinical support for a causal role rather than a purely epiphenomenal biomarker association ref [52]. In parallel, elevated VEGF and TGF-β1 in premature infants with posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus, together with CSF expression of IL-1β, IL-18, and interferon-γ, point to a broader cytokine network involving fibrosis, vascular permeability, and white-matter injury ref [12], ref [45]. These observations make anti-inflammatory or antifibrotic modulation biologically plausible.

However, translation has been disappointing. First, most human studies are associative and based on CSF biomarker enrichment rather than intervention. Second, these mediators are pleiotropic, so systemic blockade risks interfering with repair, angiogenesis, and immune regulation. Third, hydrocephalus likely reflects stage-dependent and compartment-specific processes that are difficult to reverse once tissue distortion is established ref [54], ref [55]. The biomarker literature also warns that not every elevated CSF protein is a tractable therapeutic target; for example, leucine-rich α2-glycoprotein has neurodegenerative activity in experimental systems yet primarily illustrates the complexity of distinguishing pathogenic drivers from disease correlates ref [58]. Overall, cytokine- and growth factor-directed therapy remains mechanistically compelling but clinically immature, with insufficient evidence to replace surgery.

subsections.section_title: Pharmacological and Molecular Strategies for Nonsurgical Intervention
subsections.subsection_title: Pharmacological and Molecular Strategies for Nonsurgical Intervention - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A third nonsurgical strategy has focused less on bulk CSF production and more on correcting the molecular composition of CSF or interrupting downstream injury cascades. This rationale arises from evidence that hydrocephalus is accompanied by biochemical abnormalities within CSF, including altered osmotic properties, developmental signaling, inflammatory mediators, and cell-death pathways rather than a purely mechanical disturbance alone. The concept of CSF “compensated hyperosmolarity” suggests that sustained osmotic disequilibrium may contribute to ventricular enlargement, while broader reviews of CSF biology in hydrocephalus emphasize that abnormal solute handling and signaling within the fluid compartment can itself become pathogenic ref [51], ref [43].

Biomarker studies strengthen this mechanistic view. Elevated intrathecal interleukin-6 after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage has been associated with subsequent shunt dependence, implicating persistent inflammation as a driver of failed CSF circulation recovery rather than a simple epiphenomenon ref [55]. In congenital and posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus, altered CSF aquaporin-4, dysregulated neurodevelopmental proteins, and increased soluble Fas/Fas ligand and activated caspase-3 further point to disturbed water transport, impaired developmental programs, and active apoptotic injury within the ventricular milieu ref [12], ref [29], ref [36]. These findings support interest in anti-inflammatory, anti-apoptotic, or barrier-modulating therapies, but they also indicate substantial biological heterogeneity across etiologies.

Translationally, however, molecular correction has remained difficult. Some targets may be disease-stage specific, and many reported abnormalities could be markers of established tissue injury rather than causal levers. Even more developmentally directed approaches, such as correcting fetal CSF folate imbalance to reduce congenital hydrocephalus incidence, are promising chiefly in narrowly defined contexts and are unlikely to generalize across acquired forms of the disease ref [34]. Overall, these studies are valuable for stratification and mechanistic insight, but they have not yet yielded broadly effective drug therapies, underscoring the need to distinguish actionable drivers from secondary biochemical signatures ref [43], ref [51].

subsections.section_title: Pharmacological and Molecular Strategies for Nonsurgical Intervention
subsections.subsection_title: Pharmacological and Molecular Strategies for Nonsurgical Intervention - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A recurring pharmacological theme in hydrocephalus is whether inflammatory and profibrotic signaling can be therapeutically modulated before permanent disturbance of CSF circulation is established. Human CSF studies consistently implicate transforming growth factor pathways, extracellular matrix remodeling, and cytokine activation rather than a single dominant mediator. In posthemorrhagic and secondary hydrocephalus, elevated TGF-β1, TGF-β2, procollagen-related peptides, and tenascin-C support the concept that subarachnoid or intraventricular blood products trigger fibrosis-like responses that may impair CSF absorption and predict treatment failure or later shunt dependence ref [10], ref [11], ref [31], ref [56].

The same biomarker literature also suggests that hydrocephalus-associated injury extends beyond bulk CSF flow obstruction. Neonatal high-pressure hydrocephalus has been associated with increased IL-18 and IFNγ, while broader profiling studies report altered cytokine and growth-factor milieus across hydrocephalus subtypes ref [15], ref [30]. Elevated soluble Fas points to activation of apoptotic signaling, whereas increased nerve growth factor and neurotrophin-3 may reflect endogenous but inadequate neuroprotective responses to ventricular distension and white-matter injury ref [23], ref [24]. Together, these observations provide a rationale for anti-inflammatory, anti-fibrotic, and neuroprotective drug strategies, particularly in posthemorrhagic disease.

However, these data remain largely correlative and help explain why molecular therapies have not translated into established nonsurgical treatment. Most studies are small, etiologically heterogeneous, and sample CSF after injury is already evolving; biomarkers may therefore be consequences of hydrocephalus rather than tractable upstream drivers. Moreover, the coexistence of fibrosis markers, inflammatory cytokines, apoptotic mediators, and compensatory trophic factors implies that single-target interventions are unlikely to reverse entrenched ventricular enlargement. Thus, this literature is currently more valuable for risk stratification and therapeutic target nomination than for supporting any proven stand-alone pharmacological alternative to CSF diversion ref [56], ref [10], ref [11], ref [15], ref [23], ref [24], ref [30], ref [31].

subsections.section_title: Pharmacological and Molecular Strategies for Nonsurgical Intervention
subsections.subsection_title: Pharmacological and Molecular Strategies for Nonsurgical Intervention - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A final pharmacological direction is biomarker-guided and molecularly targeted therapy, which seeks to move beyond nonspecific suppression of cerebrospinal fluid production toward intervention in discrete pathogenic pathways. Proteomic characterization of ventricular CSF from hydrocephalic patients has emphasized that hydrocephalus is accompanied by broad alterations in extracellular proteins rather than a single dominant mediator, underscoring marked biological heterogeneity and the difficulty of identifying one universally effective drug target ref [64]. More synthetic overviews of the field similarly argue that future nonsurgical therapy will depend on stratifying patients by molecular phenotype and disease mechanism, rather than treating hydrocephalus as a uniform hydrodynamic disorder ref [38].

Several candidate molecular systems have emerged, but each illustrates the translational gap between biomarker discovery and actionable therapy. Neuropeptide-related signaling, including pathways linked to the subcommissural organ, may influence ventricular development, ependymal function, and CSF flow regulation, yet the available evidence remains mechanistically suggestive rather than therapeutically mature ref [32]. Other studies have reported CSF markers of neuronal injury or oxidative stress, such as cleaved tau and 9-hydroxyoctadecadienoic acid in pediatric hydrocephalus, and older metabolic indicators such as CSF lactic dehydrogenase isoenzymes, but these markers primarily reflect downstream tissue damage and lack validated intervention points ref [17], ref [27]. Likewise, altered plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 in newborn CSF and abnormal protein expression in the subfornical organ/CSF axis of spontaneously hypertensive rats suggest roles for fibrinolytic balance and neurohumoral regulation, but causal relevance to treatable human hydrocephalus remains uncertain ref [52], ref [53].

Collectively, these studies support an important conceptual shift: molecular profiling may be more useful for patient classification, prognosis, and trial enrichment than as immediate justification for drug deployment. The recurrent reasons for limited clinical success are evident—small and heterogeneous cohorts, uncertainty about whether measured molecules are causal or epiphenomenal, poor access of candidate agents to the ventricular and periventricular compartment, and the likelihood that established hydrocephalus represents a structurally entrenched state that is only partially reversible by pharmacology ref [64], ref [32], ref [17], ref [38].

subsections.section_title: Disease Modification Beyond CSF Diversion: Neuroinflammation, Neurodegeneration, and Tissue Response
subsections.subsection_title: Disease Modification Beyond CSF Diversion: Neuroinflammation, Neurodegeneration, and Tissue Response - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
A disease-modifying view of hydrocephalus begins from the observation that ventricular enlargement is accompanied by active tissue responses rather than passive distortion alone. Experimental work shows prominent astroglial and microglial activation in hydrocephalic brain, and notably, shunting can reduce these glial responses, implying that inflammatory remodeling is dynamic and potentially therapeutically tractable rather than irreversible ref [44]. In parallel, altered aquaporin biology—especially aquaporin-4, which correlates with diffusion changes and hydrocephalus severity in rats—links disturbed water handling to parenchymal injury and raises the possibility that targeting periventricular fluid transport could complement pressure- or flow-based treatments ref [42], ref [58].

This broader framework is particularly relevant in hemorrhagic hydrocephalus, where blood products appear to act as direct biological drivers of progression. Hemoglobin and iron have been implicated in post-intraventricular hemorrhagic hydrocephalus, supporting a mechanism in which oxidative and inflammatory toxicity propagates ventricular expansion and white-matter injury beyond the initial bleed ref [51]. Consistent with this, mesenchymal stem cell therapy after severe intraventricular hemorrhage has been reported to prevent hydrocephalus in experimental settings, suggesting that immunomodulatory or trophic interventions may interrupt the secondary injury cascade before permanent CSF diversion becomes necessary ref [21].

In idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus, biomarker and biopsy studies further challenge a purely mechanical model. Cerebral biopsy findings and clinical comorbidity correlate with shunt outcome, indicating that coexisting cortical pathology may shape reversibility ref [29]. CSF studies of tau, phospho-tau181, and beta-amyloid1-42 demonstrate partial overlap with Alzheimer-type signatures while also helping discriminate idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus from primary neurodegenerative disease ref [34]. Related analyses combining CSF biomarkers with brain biopsy findings reinforce the concept that hydrocephalus may coexist with, unmask, or accelerate neurodegenerative processes, thereby defining a rationale for adjunctive therapies aimed at inflammation, proteostasis, and tissue protection in addition to CSF diversion ref [48].

subsections.section_title: Disease Modification Beyond CSF Diversion: Neuroinflammation, Neurodegeneration, and Tissue Response
subsections.subsection_title: Disease Modification Beyond CSF Diversion: Neuroinflammation, Neurodegeneration, and Tissue Response - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A biomarker-centered view of hydrocephalus supports the idea that ventricular enlargement is accompanied by active tissue injury and remodeling rather than being a purely hydrodynamic state. In idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH), proteomic profiling and targeted CSF studies have identified panels linked to axonal damage, extracellular matrix turnover, and neurodegenerative signaling, suggesting that CSF composition may capture biologically distinct disease trajectories ref [35], ref [56]. Soluble amyloid precursor protein-α has also emerged as a potentially informative marker, with diagnostic and prognostic relevance in iNPH, reinforcing the concept that altered amyloid precursor metabolism may reflect impaired periventricular tissue homeostasis rather than only coexisting Alzheimer-type pathology ref [23].

Several studies further indicate that neurodegenerative biomarkers may help stratify reversibility. Ventricular phosphorylated tau/amyloid-β1-42 ratios correlate with postoperative outcome in iNPH, implying that a stronger Alzheimer-like molecular signature may predict less favorable recovery despite CSF diversion ref [40]. Likewise, neurofilament protein levels decrease after shunt surgery in parallel with improvement in white matter pathology, providing rare evidence that at least some biomarker abnormalities track dynamic tissue rescue rather than fixed degeneration ref [24]. Pre- and post-shunt comparisons of CSF markers in secondary and idiopathic NPH similarly support the use of longitudinal biomarker change as a surrogate of treatment-responsive injury processes ref [56].

Inflammatory and profibrotic mediators broaden this framework beyond adult iNPH. In premature infants with posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus, elevated VEGF, TGF-β1, IL-1β, IL-18, and IFN-γ in CSF point to a coupled program of angiogenic signaling, cytokine activation, and white matter vulnerability ref [12], ref [45]. Comparable upregulation of TGF-β family signaling has also been reported in iNPH ref [41]. Together, these data argue that biomarker studies are not merely diagnostic adjuncts: they identify molecular pathways—axonal injury, neurodegenerative overlap, inflammation, and fibrosis—that could serve as targets for nonsurgical disease-modifying therapy and for selecting patients most likely to benefit from such interventions ref [23], ref [24], ref [35], ref [40], ref [41], ref [45], ref [56].

subsections.section_title: Disease Modification Beyond CSF Diversion: Neuroinflammation, Neurodegeneration, and Tissue Response
subsections.subsection_title: Disease Modification Beyond CSF Diversion: Neuroinflammation, Neurodegeneration, and Tissue Response - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A biomarker-based view of hydrocephalus reinforces the idea that ventricular enlargement is accompanied by active tissue injury rather than being a purely hydrodynamic disorder. In idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies repeatedly implicate protein signatures linked to neurodegeneration, including amyloid-β and tau species, while broader biomarker panels suggest overlap with impaired axonal, glial, and extracellular matrix homeostasis rather than a single disease-specific marker ref [51], ref [11], ref [13]. This has important therapeutic implications: if abnormal CSF profiles reflect ongoing and potentially modifiable tissue stress, then anti-inflammatory, anti-proteotoxic, or neuroprotective strategies could be evaluated as adjuncts to diversion rather than afterthoughts.

The same conceptual shift is evident in secondary and developmental hydrocephalus. After aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, elevated intrathecal interleukin-6 and increased CSF ferritin associate with later chronic or shunt-dependent hydrocephalus, supporting a link between inflammatory signaling, blood-breakdown products, iron handling, and persistent disturbance of CSF circulation and parenchymal recovery ref [52], ref [80]. In congenital hydrocephalus, detectable CSF aquaporin-4 suggests altered water-transport and astroglial responses at the brain-fluid interface ref [12]. In posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus of prematurity, CSF abnormalities extend beyond cytokines to proteins regulating neurodevelopment, as well as apoptotic mediators such as soluble Fas, Fas ligand, and activated caspase-3, indicating that ventricular expansion occurs in parallel with disrupted maturation and cell-death pathways ref [29], ref [36].

Taken together, these studies argue that biomarker programs in hydrocephalus should be interpreted not only diagnostically but mechanistically. Current evidence is still insufficient to define treatment-responsive molecular endotypes, and many markers lack specificity across hydrocephalus etiologies and comorbid neurodegenerative disease ref [51], ref [11]. Nevertheless, the convergence of inflammatory, iron-related, apoptotic, and neurodegenerative signals supports a disease-modification framework in which medical therapy is judged by preservation of white matter and cognition, not simply by ventricular size or shunt dependence ref [80], ref [52], ref [13], ref [29].

subsections.section_title: Disease Modification Beyond CSF Diversion: Neuroinflammation, Neurodegeneration, and Tissue Response
subsections.subsection_title: Disease Modification Beyond CSF Diversion: Neuroinflammation, Neurodegeneration, and Tissue Response - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A biomarker-centered view of hydrocephalus supports the idea that ventricular enlargement is accompanied by active extracellular-matrix remodeling, inflammation, and tissue injury rather than being a purely hydrodynamic disorder. In hemorrhagic hydrocephalus, cerebrospinal fluid tenascin-C rises before the development of chronic shunt-dependent disease after subarachnoid hemorrhage, suggesting that matrix-reactive responses may participate in the transition from acute injury to persistent CSF circulation failure ref [56]. In neonatal and preterm posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus, elevated procollagen I C-propeptide and increased TGF-β-related signaling similarly point to profibrotic remodeling within CSF pathways and periventricular tissues ref [31], ref [10], ref [11].

These observations are therapeutically relevant because they imply potentially modifiable biological cascades. Higher CSF TGF-β1 has been associated with endoscopic third ventriculostomy outcome in premature newborns with posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus, while accumulation of TGF-β2 and nitrated chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans correlates with poor neurologic outcome in preterm hydrocephalus ref [10], ref [11]. Parallel elevation of IL-18 and IFNγ in neonatal high-pressure hydrocephalus further links inflammatory activation to white-matter vulnerability, reinforcing the rationale for anti-inflammatory or anti-fibrotic adjuncts aimed at limiting secondary tissue damage rather than only lowering CSF pressure ref [15].

Biomarker studies in chronic adult hydrocephalus also indicate overlap with neurodegenerative processes. CSF profiles can distinguish idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus from Alzheimer’s disease, yet they also reveal partial convergence in markers associated with axonal injury and impaired protein clearance ref [16]. Pilot comparisons between idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus and subarachnoid hemorrhage-induced chronic hydrocephalus suggest that distinct etiologies may share downstream injury signatures despite different initiating events ref [22]. Consistent with this, increased CSF total tau has been reported in pediatric hydrocephalus, indicating that neuronal or axonal damage is not restricted to degenerative adult syndromes ref [29]. Overall, these biomarker patterns strengthen the case for disease-modifying trials targeting inflammation, fibrosis, and neuroprotection alongside CSF diversion.

subsections.section_title: Disease Modification Beyond CSF Diversion: Neuroinflammation, Neurodegeneration, and Tissue Response
subsections.subsection_title: Disease Modification Beyond CSF Diversion: Neuroinflammation, Neurodegeneration, and Tissue Response - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A practical implication of viewing hydrocephalus as a progressive tissue disorder is that biomarker discovery may help identify patients in whom adjunctive medical therapy should target neuronal injury, oxidative stress, or persistent gliotic remodeling rather than CSF volume alone. Ventricular CSF proteomic profiling in hydrocephalic patients demonstrates that the hydrocephalic milieu contains far more than pressure-related dilutional changes, instead revealing broad alterations in proteins linked to inflammation, extracellular matrix turnover, and neural injury ref [64]. Earlier biochemical studies similarly detected shifts in CSF lactic dehydrogenase isoenzymes, supporting the concept that hydrocephalus is accompanied by metabolically active tissue damage rather than a purely passive hydrodynamic state ref [27].

The neurodegenerative dimension is especially important when considering long-term outcome and treatment responsiveness. In pediatric hydrocephalus, elevations of cleaved tau and 9-hydroxyoctadecadienoic acid suggest concurrent axonal injury and lipid peroxidation, implicating oxidative and degenerative pathways as plausible therapeutic targets ref [17]. More broadly, research perspectives have emphasized that hydrocephalus intersects with chronic white-matter injury, altered CSF composition, and secondary molecular cascades that may persist despite technically adequate diversion ref [38]. Within this framework, biomarkers are not only diagnostic adjuncts; they may serve as pharmacodynamic readouts for disease-modifying interventions.

The current limitation is translational rather than conceptual. Available biomarker studies remain heterogeneous, often small, and largely observational, so they do not yet define a validated treatment algorithm. Nevertheless, proteomic, enzymatic, and neurodegeneration-associated CSF signatures collectively support a shift from asking whether diversion normalizes ventricular size to asking whether combined surgical and medical strategies can attenuate ongoing parenchymal injury ref [64], ref [17], ref [27], ref [38]. This biomarker-guided perspective provides a rational bridge toward future trials of anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and neuroprotective therapies in hydrocephalus.

subsections.section_title: Nonsurgical Management Across Hydrocephalus Subtypes and Clinical Contexts
subsections.subsection_title: Nonsurgical Management Across Hydrocephalus Subtypes and Clinical Contexts - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
In posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus of prematurity and related neonatal intraventricular hemorrhage settings, nonsurgical strategies are best understood as prevention or temporizing interventions rather than definitive therapy. Mechanistically, blood-breakdown products appear central: hemoglobin and iron have been implicated in ventricular enlargement and secondary tissue injury after neonatal intraventricular hemorrhage, supporting efforts aimed at early clearance of intraventricular blood and attenuation of toxicity ref [51]. Consistent with this rationale, a randomized trial comparing ventricular “brain-washing” with fluid tapping in preterm infants explicitly targeted prevention of progressive hydrocephalus after hemorrhage, illustrating that subtype-specific medical management may focus on modifying the intraventricular milieu rather than on cerebrospinal fluid diversion alone ref [23].

Biologic therapies remain investigational but are particularly relevant in this neonatal context. Experimental work with mesenchymal stem cells reported prevention of hydrocephalus after severe intraventricular hemorrhage, suggesting that anti-inflammatory or reparative approaches could become adjuncts in high-risk infants if safety, timing, and durability are clarified in clinical translation ref [21]. By contrast, pharmacologic suppression of cerebrospinal fluid production has only limited, niche support. The use of acetazolamide to decrease cerebrospinal fluid production has been described in chronically ventilated patients with ventriculopleural shunts, but this experience is better viewed as context-specific adjunctive management than as a broadly effective standalone treatment for infant posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus ref [55].

A different nonsurgical paradigm applies in idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH), where lumbar drainage-based tests are not therapeutic in the durable sense but are highly relevant to management decisions. The cerebrospinal fluid tap test has value in predicting shunt responsiveness, thereby functioning as a diagnostic-prognostic tool that guides whether surgical treatment is likely to help ref [38]. Likewise, cerebrospinal fluid pulse pressure amplitude measured during lumbar infusion has been reported to predict response to shunting, emphasizing that, in slowly progressive adult hydrocephalus, “nonsurgical management” often consists of physiological stratification and selective referral rather than disease-modifying drug therapy ref [56]. Together, these examples show that the role of nonsurgical approaches varies sharply by subtype: preventive and temporizing in neonatal hemorrhagic disease, but primarily triaging and adjunctive in iNPH ref [23], ref [38], ref [56].

subsections.section_title: Nonsurgical Management Across Hydrocephalus Subtypes and Clinical Contexts
subsections.subsection_title: Nonsurgical Management Across Hydrocephalus Subtypes and Clinical Contexts - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
In idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH), truly disease-modifying nonsurgical therapy remains unproven; accordingly, medical management is best framed as diagnostic stratification, symptomatic support, and peri-decisional optimization rather than definitive treatment. This context differs from rapidly progressive pediatric or posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus, because the principal nonsurgical need in iNPH is often to distinguish potentially reversible hydrocephalic gait-cognitive syndrome from neurodegenerative mimics and to identify patients most likely to benefit from shunting ref [89], ref [17].

CSF dynamic testing and pressure manipulation therefore function as a quasi-therapeutic trial in iNPH. Studies of CSF drainage and infusion-based assessment support the value of temporary CSF removal for evaluating reversibility of symptoms, while methodological work on cerebral blood flow changes during CSF pressure manipulation suggests that at least part of the clinical response reflects hemodynamic recruitment rather than simple ventricular decompression alone ref [17], ref [18]. Although such interventions are not durable treatments, they can justify temporizing conservative care in frail patients while clarifying prognosis and procedural candidacy.

Biomarker-driven nonsurgical management is also particularly relevant in iNPH. Comparative CSF studies indicate that protein profiles may help separate iNPH from Alzheimer disease and mild cognitive impairment, including patterns involving soluble amyloid precursor protein-α, beta-trace protein, proteomic signatures, and tau/amyloid ratios ref [89], ref [23], ref [35], ref [40], ref [53]. Prognostically, ventricular neurofilament reduction after shunting parallels white matter improvement, reinforcing its potential utility as a monitoring rather than primary therapeutic marker ref [24]. Overall, in iNPH the main role of nonsurgical management is adjunctive: refining diagnosis, estimating shunt responsiveness, tracking biological effect, and supporting patients who are poor surgical candidates or require delayed intervention ref [23], ref [24], ref [40].

subsections.section_title: Nonsurgical Management Across Hydrocephalus Subtypes and Clinical Contexts
subsections.subsection_title: Nonsurgical Management Across Hydrocephalus Subtypes and Clinical Contexts - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
In idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH), nonsurgical management is not a definitive alternative to shunting, but it has an important role in patient selection, prognostic stratification, and short-term symptom assessment. Contemporary diagnostic frameworks emphasize that because gait, cognitive, and urinary symptoms overlap with neurodegenerative disease, medical evaluation is centered on identifying potentially reversible physiology rather than providing durable pharmacologic control ref [9]. In this context, CSF tap testing and temporary lumbar drainage function as nonsurgical trial interventions: they do not treat the disorder long term, but they can clarify whether symptom improvement is likely after diversion ref [11], ref [41].

The strongest evidence for these temporizing approaches comes from studies linking CSF hydrodynamics to shunt responsiveness. Abnormal CSF dynamic profiles, including impaired outflow characteristics, have been associated with later benefit from diversion ref [28]. Quantitative phase-contrast MRI has also been explored as a noninvasive adjunct to identify patients with flow abnormalities compatible with NPH physiology, although it is best interpreted alongside clinical testing rather than as a stand-alone determinant ref [33]. External continuous lumbar drainage appears to provide higher predictive value than a single tap test in some series, particularly when symptom fluctuation or equivocal presentation complicates decision-making ref [41].

Biomarker studies further refine this nonsurgical evaluation pathway. Reviews of CSF biomarkers in iNPH highlight the value of amyloid-β and tau profiles primarily for distinguishing iNPH from Alzheimer-spectrum pathology and for estimating the likelihood of postoperative improvement ref [93], ref [11]. More specifically, CSF amyloid-β and total tau have been reported to predict favorable surgical outcomes in selected patients ref [13]. These tools should be understood as adjuncts rather than therapies, especially since long-term outcome data still support shunting as the main effective treatment for appropriately selected patients ref [15]. Thus, in iNPH, the principal contribution of nonsurgical management is careful diagnostic enrichment and temporizing assessment, not disease modification.

subsections.section_title: Nonsurgical Management Across Hydrocephalus Subtypes and Clinical Contexts
subsections.subsection_title: Nonsurgical Management Across Hydrocephalus Subtypes and Clinical Contexts - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
In posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus of prematurity, nonsurgical care is best understood as temporizing and pathobiology-informed rather than definitively curative. Human neonatal studies indicate that this subtype commonly combines intraventricular obstruction with impaired CSF absorption, helping explain why drug-only strategies rarely provide durable control once ventricular enlargement is established ref [57]. During this window, serial drainage remains the principal nonsurgical intervention, used to stabilize intracranial physiology, preserve cerebral perfusion, and delay permanent diversion when feasible; Doppler data showing altered cerebral blood-flow velocities before and after CSF drainage support this rationale ref [25].

Biomarker work further suggests why outcomes vary and why medical modulation remains attractive but unproven. Elevated CSF TGF-β1, TGF-β2, nitrated chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans, procollagen I C-propeptide, and pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-18 and IFNγ all point to a milieu of fibrosis, extracellular-matrix remodeling, and neuroinflammation in neonatal posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus ref [10], ref [11], ref [15], ref [31]. These markers also have potential stratification value: higher TGF-β1 has been linked to poorer endoscopic third ventriculostomy outcome in premature newborns, underscoring that biologically aggressive communicating disease may be less amenable to CSF-bypass procedures and even less likely to respond to pharmacologic suppression alone ref [10].

A related but distinct context is hydrocephalus after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage in adults, where nonsurgical management may include prolonged CSF drainage protocols during the acute phase. Clinical observations suggest that drainage duration can influence later symptomatic vasospasm and late hydrocephalus risk, although such strategies are still supportive rather than disease-modifying ref [38]. Concurrently, rising CSF tenascin-C before chronic shunt-dependent hydrocephalus highlights extracellular-matrix activation as a possible predictor of transition from acute blood-related CSF disturbance to persistent hydrocephalus ref [31]. Across both neonatal posthemorrhagic and post-subarachnoid hemorrhage settings, current evidence therefore supports nonsurgical therapy mainly as temporization, physiologic support, and biomarker-guided risk assessment, not as a reliable substitute for definitive CSF diversion.

subsections.section_title: Nonsurgical Management Across Hydrocephalus Subtypes and Clinical Contexts
subsections.subsection_title: Nonsurgical Management Across Hydrocephalus Subtypes and Clinical Contexts - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
In adult chronic hydrocephalus, particularly idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH), “nonsurgical management” is usually best understood not as durable pharmacotherapy but as diagnostic stratification, temporizing observation, and management of physiological contributors that may modify symptoms or apparent shunt responsiveness. Work on CSF hydrodynamics emphasizes that this subtype is characterized less by simple CSF overproduction than by complex disturbances in outflow, compliance, and venous-CSF coupling, making patient selection and monitoring central components of medical management rather than optional preliminaries ref [11], ref [23].

Accordingly, infusion-based assessment of CSF outflow conductance and related parameters has become a key adjunctive tool in chronic adult hydrocephalus. Methodological studies using adaptive observers, oscillating pressure infusion, and analyses of resting pressure effects show that estimates of outflow conductance are technically feasible but sensitive to assumptions, baseline pressure, and model structure; these factors limit overinterpretation of single test values when deciding between conservative follow-up and surgery ref [40], ref [45], ref [46], ref [47]. Earlier work also linked chronic hydrocephalus to impaired absorption at the cranial vertex, while questioning whether the primary abnormality lies in arachnoid granulations or elevated venous pressure, reinforcing the rationale for addressing systemic and vascular comorbidity during nonsurgical care ref [10].

Clinically, prognostic studies in iNPH suggest that hydrodynamic measures should be integrated with phenotype rather than used in isolation, since clinical characteristics and CSF dynamic parameters jointly influence the likelihood of benefit from shunting ref [100]. Thus, in this adult subgroup, nonsurgical management is mainly supportive and triage-oriented: optimize cardiovascular and venous factors, monitor gait-cognitive-urinary trajectories, and use imaging and hydrodynamic testing to identify those in whom conservative management is reasonable versus those unlikely to improve without surgery ref [100], ref [11], ref [23].

subsections.section_title: Diagnostics, Biomarkers, and Imaging for Therapeutic Stratification and Monitoring
subsections.subsection_title: Diagnostics, Biomarkers, and Imaging for Therapeutic Stratification and Monitoring - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
For nonsurgical therapy development in hydrocephalus, especially idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH), patient selection depends on combining dynamic physiological tests with biomarkers that separate treatable CSF-circulatory dysfunction from neurodegenerative mimics. The CSF tap test remains a pragmatic enrichment tool because short-term gait or cognitive improvement after large-volume drainage provides a clinically interpretable surrogate of reversibility, although its sensitivity is imperfect and it is best used within a multimodal framework rather than as a stand-alone gatekeeper ref [38]. Infusion-based assessment of CSF outflow resistance adds a more mechanistic dimension by quantifying impaired absorptive reserve, thereby identifying patients in whom interventions targeting CSF dynamics may have the greatest biological plausibility ref [40].

Phase-contrast MRI of aqueductal CSF flow has particular value as a noninvasive stratification marker. Technical validation studies established the feasibility of measuring aqueductal stroke volume and flow patterns in vivo, and subsequent work suggested that elevated flow rates may help distinguish iNPH from other causes of ventriculomegaly and may also predict response to CSF diversion ref [16], ref [36]. Related pressure-pulsatility metrics obtained during lumbar infusion, including CSF pulse pressure amplitude, further support the concept that abnormal craniospinal compliance and pulsatile hydrodynamics are clinically informative and may outperform static pressure measures for response prediction ref [56].

Fluid biomarkers are most useful when interpreted as indicators of comorbidity burden rather than as disease-specific signatures. Classical Alzheimer-related analytes—total tau, phospho-tau181, and Aβ1-42—show discriminatory value between iNPH and Alzheimer’s disease, helping identify patients whose symptoms may be less amenable to CSF-directed therapy ref [34]. Concordantly, studies integrating CSF biomarker panels with cortical biopsy findings indicate that coexisting Alzheimer-type pathology is common in iNPH and materially influences expected treatment benefit ref [48]. Taken together, tap testing, outflow-resistance and pulsatility measurements, phase-contrast MRI, and neurodegeneration-oriented CSF biomarkers form a complementary diagnostic set for precision stratification and for monitoring biological response in trials of nonsurgical therapy ref [38], ref [40], ref [16], ref [36], ref [34], ref [48], ref [56].

subsections.section_title: Diagnostics, Biomarkers, and Imaging for Therapeutic Stratification and Monitoring
subsections.subsection_title: Diagnostics, Biomarkers, and Imaging for Therapeutic Stratification and Monitoring - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
Cerebrospinal fluid biomarker panels are particularly valuable for therapeutic stratification in idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH), where symptomatic overlap with Alzheimer’s disease and mild cognitive impairment complicates selection for nonsurgical or adjunctive interventions. Comparative studies indicate that combined assessment of CSF and blood-flow related measures can aid differential diagnosis, helping distinguish iNPH from neurodegenerative mimics that may respond poorly to hydrocephalus-directed strategies ref [91]. Within CSF, lipocalin-type prostaglandin D synthase (beta-trace) has been proposed as a useful diagnostic marker for normal pressure hydrocephalus, while soluble amyloid precursor protein-α has shown both diagnostic and prognostic potential, suggesting that biomarker-informed enrichment may improve cohort homogeneity in trials ref [53], ref [23].

Proteomic approaches further support the idea that iNPH is biologically heterogeneous rather than a purely imaging-defined syndrome. Exploratory CSF proteomics has identified candidate diagnostic signatures beyond conventional amyloid and tau analytes, although these findings still require analytical standardization and external validation before routine clinical deployment ref [35]. At the same time, ventricular phosphorylated tau/amyloid-β1-42 ratio appears to track outcome in iNPH, implying that concomitant neurodegenerative pathology may modify expected treatment response and should be incorporated into stratification algorithms rather than treated as incidental comorbidity ref [40].

For monitoring biological response, longitudinal biomarker change may be as important as baseline classification. Neurofilament protein levels in ventricular CSF decrease after shunt surgery in parallel with improvement in white matter pathology, supporting axonal injury markers as potential pharmacodynamic readouts for therapies aimed at reducing tissue stress or restoring periventricular integrity ref [24]. Similarly, studies measuring CSF markers before and after shunting in both secondary and idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus show that biomarker trajectories can reflect treatment-related physiological shifts ref [56]. Taken together, these data argue for integrating diagnostic, prognostic, and response biomarkers into precision trial design, while recognizing that assay harmonization and compartment-specific sampling remain major barriers to translation.

subsections.section_title: Diagnostics, Biomarkers, and Imaging for Therapeutic Stratification and Monitoring
subsections.subsection_title: Diagnostics, Biomarkers, and Imaging for Therapeutic Stratification and Monitoring - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A practical stratification framework for nonsurgical therapy should combine physiological testing with structural and flow imaging rather than rely on a single marker. In idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH), diagnostic and prognostic studies indicate that no individual test is sufficiently definitive, but multimodal assessment improves identification of biologically coherent patient subgroups and provides a baseline against which pharmacologic response can be judged ref [9]. Infusion-based measurements of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) outflow conductance and related hydrodynamic parameters are particularly relevant because they probe the compensatory reserve of the CSF system, a mechanistic target for several nonsurgical strategies ref [16], ref [28].

Among physiological tools, constant-pressure infusion methods offer a quantitative estimate of outflow conductance with real-time reliability assessment, which is attractive for both enrollment and longitudinal monitoring in trials ref [16]. Earlier work linking CSF dynamics to shunt responsiveness supports the broader principle that altered hydrodynamics reflect clinically meaningful disease biology even when the intervention is not surgical ref [28]. Likewise, diagnostic/prognostic syntheses in iNPH emphasize the value of the CSF tap test as a functional stress test, especially when interpreted alongside CSF biomarker profiles rather than as a binary standalone screen ref [9], ref [11].

Imaging can further refine this scheme. Automatic volumetry of CSF spaces provides objective characterization of ventricular and extra-axial compartment anatomy, reducing observer dependence and enabling quantitative follow-up ref [21]. Phase-contrast MRI studies of aqueductal flow have also been proposed to identify patients with NPH physiology and, in some cohorts, to predict treatment responsiveness, although such metrics should be interpreted cautiously because flow abnormalities may reflect both cause and compensation ref [33]. Fluid biomarkers can then add pathobiological context: CSF amyloid-β and total tau have been associated with outcome heterogeneity in iNPH ref [13], while broader biomarker reviews highlight their utility mainly in distinguishing hydrocephalic syndromes from overlapping neurodegenerative processes and in enriching trial populations rather than serving as disease-specific surrogates ref [18].

subsections.section_title: Diagnostics, Biomarkers, and Imaging for Therapeutic Stratification and Monitoring
subsections.subsection_title: Diagnostics, Biomarkers, and Imaging for Therapeutic Stratification and Monitoring - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A practical stratification framework for nonsurgical therapy should not rely on any single test, but instead combine structural MRI, diffusion metrics, flow imaging, and CSF chemistry to estimate reversibility of periventricular injury and to exclude major mimics. In idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH), cortical thinning has been linked to tap-test responsiveness, suggesting that morphometric readouts may capture the balance between chronic damage and recoverable dysfunction ref [13]. Likewise, voxel-based morphometry of the disproportionate CSF space pattern can improve differential diagnosis, helping distinguish iNPH from other dementing or atrophic states that are less likely to benefit from hydrocephalus-directed medical interventions ref [42].

Biochemical markers may further enrich for biologically responsive patients. Improvement after CSF drainage has been associated with N-acetyl-aspartate levels, supporting the concept that metabolic integrity markers can serve as surrogate indicators of tissue salvageability rather than diagnosis alone ref [14]. CSF biomarker panels also assist in separating iNPH from Alzheimer’s disease and from secondary chronic hydrocephalus after subarachnoid hemorrhage, contexts in which therapeutic mechanisms and expected responses may differ substantially ref [16], ref [22]. For trial design, such comparative biomarker profiling is especially relevant when testing agents aimed at neuroinflammation, glymphatic transport, or CSF production, because apparent clinical overlap may conceal distinct underlying biology ref [16], ref [22].

Monitoring should similarly emphasize dynamic change. Diffusion-weighted imaging demonstrates decreased tissue water diffusion after CSF diversion in infants with hydrocephalus, indicating that ADC-type measures may provide a quantitative marker of parenchymal response ref [21]. More generally, apparent diffusion coefficient and CSF flow measurements have shown complementary value in hydrocephalus assessment ref [50], while MRI flow-void changes after shunting in post-traumatic hydrocephalus correlate with outcome and illustrate the potential of serial flow-sensitive imaging as a pharmacodynamic endpoint ref [47]. Although these studies arise largely from procedural interventions, the same multimodal biomarkers are highly transferable to nonsurgical trials, where they could identify target engagement before overt clinical improvement becomes measurable ref [21], ref [47], ref [50].

subsections.section_title: Diagnostics, Biomarkers, and Imaging for Therapeutic Stratification and Monitoring
subsections.subsection_title: Diagnostics, Biomarkers, and Imaging for Therapeutic Stratification and Monitoring - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
For nonsurgical therapy, the most useful monitoring framework is multimodal rather than biomarker-only. CSF hydrodynamic testing can identify the dominant physiological bottleneck—impaired outflow, altered compliance, or disturbed pulsatility—and therefore helps distinguish patients in whom pharmacologic reduction of CSF production is unlikely to suffice from those with potentially modifiable flow abnormalities. Reviews of CSF diagnostics emphasize that hydrocephalus is a disorder of coupled pressure–flow regulation, not simply ventricular size, and infusion-based measures of outflow conductance provide quantitative parameters that can be followed longitudinally in trials ref [11], ref [40]. Prognostic studies in idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus likewise show that clinical phenotype gains predictive value when interpreted together with CSF hydrodynamic parameters rather than in isolation ref [33].

Advanced imaging should be integrated with these physiological measurements. Contemporary MR approaches visualize intracranial CSF spaces and circulation with greater anatomical specificity, improving phenotypic classification beyond routine ventriculomegaly metrics ref [65], ref [23]. Such imaging is particularly relevant when considering nonsurgical approaches aimed at modifying production, absorption, or venous/lymphatic egress, because chronic hydrocephalus may reflect absorption block near the vertex, elevated venous pressure, or mixed mechanisms that are not therapeutically equivalent ref [10]. In this context, imaging can serve both as an enrichment tool at baseline and as a pharmacodynamic readout when repeated after treatment initiation ref [65], ref [23].

Fluid biomarkers remain complementary but potentially informative for biological response monitoring. Proteomic profiling of ventricular CSF in hydrocephalic patients demonstrates that the disease leaves a measurable molecular signature spanning inflammation, extracellular matrix remodeling, and tissue injury pathways ref [64]. Smaller candidate-marker studies further suggest that neuronal injury and lipid peroxidation markers, including cleaved tau and 9-hydroxyoctadecadienoic acid in pediatric hydrocephalus, may capture aspects of ongoing parenchymal stress not visible on routine imaging ref [17]. Overall, precision stratification for nonsurgical therapy will likely require composite panels that combine molecular readouts with hydrodynamic and imaging measures, rather than expecting any single test to function as a universal selector or surrogate endpoint ref [64], ref [33], ref [11], ref [40].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Evidence, Translational Challenges, and Future Directions in Nonsurgical Therapy
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Evidence, Translational Challenges, and Future Directions in Nonsurgical Therapy - Subtopic 1
subsections.content:
Clinical evidence for nonsurgical therapy remains sparse and heterogeneous, with most interventions evaluated either as temporizing measures or as adjuncts to procedural care rather than as stand-alone disease-modifying treatments. In neonates with posthemorrhagic ventricular dilatation, the strongest human evidence among current candidates comes from procedural trials aimed at reducing the biological drivers of hydrocephalus progression. A randomized trial comparing ventricular lavage (“brain-washing”) with tapping fluid in preterm infants suggested that removal of blood breakdown products may modify the subsequent course of hydrocephalus, but this strategy is only partly “nonsurgical” and does not establish a broadly deployable pharmacologic therapy ref [23].

By contrast, attempts to directly suppress cerebrospinal fluid production have yielded limited and context-specific support. Physiologic studies indicate that CSF production may already be downregulated in chronic hydrocephalus, raising concern that secretion-targeted drugs could have modest efficacy in established disease ref [52]. Clinical use of acetazolamide has therefore remained anecdotal or highly selective, as illustrated by reports in chronically ventilated patients with ventriculopleural shunts rather than robust hydrocephalus cohorts ref [55]. Similarly, aquaporin-focused therapies are mechanistically attractive, but the translational path is still preclinical because aquaporins regulate water movement in complex, compartment-specific ways that could be either protective or maladaptive depending on stage and etiology ref [58].

More recent biologic strategies, particularly mesenchymal stem cell therapy after severe intraventricular hemorrhage, have generated substantial interest because they target inflammation and secondary injury rather than CSF dynamics alone ref [21]. Yet these data remain early-phase and must be interpreted alongside the field’s broader reliance on surrogate endpoints. Even in idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus, where tap testing and infusion-derived pulse amplitude can enrich for shunt responsiveness, these tools primarily guide surgical selection rather than validate medical efficacy ref [38], ref [56]. Overall, the present evidence base suggests that nonsurgical treatment is most plausible in narrowly defined windows—especially early posthemorrhagic disease—but remains constrained by small studies, mixed phenotypes, and the absence of validated pharmacodynamic biomarkers ref [21], ref [23], ref [52].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Evidence, Translational Challenges, and Future Directions in Nonsurgical Therapy
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Evidence, Translational Challenges, and Future Directions in Nonsurgical Therapy - Subtopic 2
subsections.content:
A major translational bottleneck for nonsurgical hydrocephalus therapy is the absence of validated biomarkers that can reliably stratify patients, distinguish pathogenic subtypes, and serve as pharmacodynamic readouts. Most available data come from idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH), where candidate cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) markers—including soluble amyloid precursor protein-α, beta-trace protein, tau/Aβ-related indices, and broader proteomic signatures—have shown diagnostic or prognostic associations, but not consistent enough performance for routine therapeutic decision-making ref [23], ref [35], ref [40], ref [53]. The biomarker literature is further complicated by overlap with neurodegenerative disease biology, especially Alzheimer-type pathology, making it difficult to determine whether a marker reflects hydrocephalus mechanisms, comorbidity, or irreversible parenchymal injury ref [40].

Mechanistically oriented studies also suggest that CSF biomarkers may capture distinct biological axes relevant to drug development. Elevated TGF-β signaling in iNPH supports a role for fibrosis, extracellular matrix remodeling, or impaired CSF compartment compliance, while pre/post-shunt studies indicate that at least some CSF markers are dynamically modulated by diversion, implying potential utility as treatment-response indicators rather than static diagnostic labels ref [41], ref [56]. Proteomic analyses likewise imply that hydrocephalus is biologically heterogeneous rather than a single analyte-defined disorder ref [35]. These observations align with broader reconsiderations of hydrocephalus pathogenesis and CSF physiology, which increasingly emphasize distributed disturbances in production, flow, absorption, interstitial exchange, and tissue response rather than a simple plumbing defect ref [54], ref [55].

For future nonsurgical trials, biomarker work must move beyond exploratory cross-sectional studies. Priorities include standardized sampling compartments, longitudinal designs, integration with imaging and clinical phenotyping, and explicit separation of predictive, prognostic, and mechanistic biomarkers. Without that framework, candidate therapies will continue to be tested in biologically mixed populations, obscuring efficacy signals even when the underlying target is valid ref [23], ref [53], ref [54], ref [55].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Evidence, Translational Challenges, and Future Directions in Nonsurgical Therapy
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Evidence, Translational Challenges, and Future Directions in Nonsurgical Therapy - Subtopic 3
subsections.content:
A central translational challenge for nonsurgical hydrocephalus therapy is the absence of validated enrichment markers that can identify biologically homogeneous patients and provide early readouts of response. Work in idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH) shows that prognosis is currently inferred from a patchwork of clinical assessment, CSF drainage tests, hydrodynamic studies, imaging, and biomarker sampling rather than from any single robust predictor ref [9], ref [28], ref [41]. This fragmented diagnostic architecture has immediate implications for drug development: if trial populations contain mixtures of true CSF-circulatory disease, neurodegenerative comorbidity, and advanced irreversible tissue injury, even a mechanistically active medical therapy may appear ineffective.

The available literature suggests that multimodal stratification is more promising than reliance on any isolated test. CSF biomarker studies indicate that amyloid-β and tau profiles may help separate iNPH from overlapping Alzheimer-type pathology and may carry prognostic information for intervention response ref [22], ref [11], ref [13], ref [57]. In parallel, phase-contrast MRI and CSF dynamic measurements have been explored as physiologic markers of disturbed flow and shunt responsiveness, while external lumbar drainage remains one of the more practical functional tests for reversibility ref [28], ref [33], ref [41]. However, across these approaches, thresholds are inconsistent, cohorts are small, and endpoint definitions vary, limiting external validity.

For future nonsurgical trials, these observations argue for biomarker-guided study design rather than empiric treatment of broadly defined hydrocephalus syndromes. Priority should be given to prospective protocols that combine CSF molecular markers, standardized drainage response testing, and quantitative flow imaging to define endotypes and to distinguish reversible CSF-dynamic dysfunction from fixed neurodegeneration ref [22], ref [9], ref [33], ref [57]. Such an approach would not only improve patient selection but also provide surrogate measures needed to determine whether a candidate therapy is engaging its target before clinical deterioration becomes irreversible.

subsections.section_title: Clinical Evidence, Translational Challenges, and Future Directions in Nonsurgical Therapy
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Evidence, Translational Challenges, and Future Directions in Nonsurgical Therapy - Subtopic 4
subsections.content:
A major translational bottleneck in nonsurgical hydrocephalus therapy is the absence of validated biomarkers that can reliably identify biologically distinct disease states, predict progression, or enrich trials for treatment-responsive patients. Existing cerebrospinal fluid studies instead suggest marked heterogeneity across etiologies. In neonatal and posthemorrhagic hydrocephalus, profiles consistent with fibrosis, extracellular matrix remodeling, and inflammation have been reported, including elevations in procollagen I C-propeptide, TGF-β-related signals, nitrated chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans, IL-18, and IFNγ, while tenascin-C rises before chronic shunt-dependent hydrocephalus after subarachnoid hemorrhage ref [31], ref [10], ref [11], ref [15], ref [63]. These observations support biologically plausible therapeutic targets, but they do not yet constitute clinically actionable companion biomarkers.

The main limitation is that most studies are small, single-center, and observational, with substantial variation in sampling site, timing relative to hemorrhage or ventricular enlargement, and clinical end points. Mechanistic interpretation is also complicated by mixed pathophysiology: human neonatal hydrocephaly reflects both CSF obstruction and impaired absorption rather than a single uniform process ref [57]. Cross-etiology comparisons reinforce this concern; even pilot biomarker studies contrasting idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus with subarachnoid hemorrhage-related chronic hydrocephalus indicate that shared ventricular enlargement can mask distinct underlying molecular programs ref [22]. Likewise, associations between CSF TGF-β1 levels and ETV outcome are provocative, but they remain insufficient for patient selection without external validation and standardized thresholds ref [10].

Future progress will require biomarker programs designed for translation rather than description: prospective longitudinal sampling, harmonized assay platforms, prespecified outcomes, and integration with imaging and CSF hydrodynamics. Priority should be given to multimarker panels that capture fibrosis, inflammation, and barrier dysfunction together, because single-analyte approaches are unlikely to resolve hydrocephalus heterogeneity ref [11], ref [15], ref [31]. If such panels can stratify patients at risk for progressive posthemorrhagic or post-subarachnoid hydrocephalus, they could finally enable mechanism-based trials of anti-inflammatory or anti-fibrotic nonsurgical therapies and reduce the current dependence on empiric, surgery-centered management ref [63], ref [22], ref [57].

subsections.section_title: Clinical Evidence, Translational Challenges, and Future Directions in Nonsurgical Therapy
subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Evidence, Translational Challenges, and Future Directions in Nonsurgical Therapy - Subtopic 5
subsections.content:
A major future direction for nonsurgical hydrocephalus therapy is the development of quantitative, mechanism-linked biomarkers that can support patient stratification, pharmacodynamic monitoring, and early go/no-go decisions in trials. Current evidence suggests that hydrocephalus is biologically heterogeneous: ventricular CSF proteomic profiling in affected patients reveals complex molecular signatures rather than a single dominant pathway, while pediatric studies of cleaved tau and lipid oxidation products similarly indicate mixed patterns of injury and stress responses rather than disease-specific markers ref [64], ref [17]. This heterogeneity helps explain why empiric drug approaches have translated poorly and argues for biomarker-guided enrollment rather than syndrome-based treatment alone.

Progress will also depend on better integration of biomarkers with quantitative physiology and imaging. Experimental work measuring CSF volume in hydrocephalic rats, together with MRI tracer studies of drainage pathways in hydrocephalic guinea pigs, shows that ventricular enlargement, altered clearance, and disturbed transport are measurable and may not map onto a single mechanism ref [35], ref [22]. In parallel, theoretical and systems-based approaches provide a framework for interpreting these multidimensional abnormalities, and adaptive observer methods for estimating outflow conductance suggest that clinically relevant hydrodynamic parameters can be extracted more robustly than with static descriptors alone ref [39], ref [40].

Looking ahead, translational success will likely require multimodal trial platforms that combine molecular CSF markers, imaging of transport and drainage, and computational estimates of intracranial dynamics. Early work using neural-network-based noninvasive CSF pressure estimation points toward scalable monitoring strategies, although external validation and generalizability remain substantial concerns ref [54]. More broadly, the field has already recognized the need to move beyond simplistic production-versus-absorption models toward integrated, testable pathophysiologic frameworks ref [38]. For nonsurgical therapy, the implication is clear: future studies should prioritize longitudinal phenotyping, standardized outcome measures, and mechanism-matched interventions rather than expecting a single agent to benefit all forms of hydrocephalus ref [38], ref [39].
